solution:
Convert the side to SI before cubing.

\(1\,\text{cm} = 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\)

\(V = (\text{side})^{3} = (10^{-2}\,\text{m})^{3} = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

The volume of the cube is \(10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}\).

For a SOLID cylinder the total surface area includes the curved surface and BOTH flat ends:

\(S = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^{2} = 2\pi r (r + h)\)

With \(r = 2.0\,\text{cm}\) and \(h = 10.0\,\text{cm}\),

\(S = 2\pi (2.0)(2.0 + 10.0) = 48\pi = 150.8\,\text{cm}^{2}\)

Converting, \(1\,\text{cm}^{2} = (10\,\text{mm})^{2} = 10^{2}\,\text{mm}^{2}\), so

\(S = 150.8 \times 10^{2}\,\text{mm}^{2} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\,\text{mm}^{2}\)

The surface area is \(1.5 \times 10^{4}\,\text{mm}^{2}\) (2 significant figures, set by \(r = 2.0\,\text{cm}\)).

Convert the speed to SI:

\(18\,\text{km h}^{-1} = 18 \times \dfrac{10^{3}\,\text{m}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Distance covered in \(1\,\text{s}\) is \(x = v t = 5 \times 1 = 5\,\text{m}\).

The vehicle covers \(5\,\text{m}\) in \(1\,\text{s}\).

Relative density is the ratio of the density of the substance to that of water, so it is dimensionless:

\(\rho_{\text{lead}} = 11.3 \times \rho_{\text{water}}\)

Taking \(\rho_{\text{water}} = 1\,\text{g cm}^{-3}\),

\(\rho_{\text{lead}} = 11.3\,\text{g cm}^{-3}\)

Converting, \(1\,\text{g cm}^{-3} = \dfrac{10^{-3}\,\text{kg}}{10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}} = 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), so

\(\rho_{\text{lead}} = 11.3 \times 10^{3} = 1.13 \times 10^{4}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)

The density of lead is \(11.3\,\text{g cm}^{-3}\) or \(1.13 \times 10^{4}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).

Replace each SI unit by its CGS equivalent:

\(1\,\text{kg} = 10^{3}\,\text{g}\) and \(1\,\text{m}^{2} = (10^{2}\,\text{cm})^{2} = 10^{4}\,\text{cm}^{2}\); the second is unchanged.

\(1\,\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2} = (10^{3})(10^{4})\,\text{g cm}^{2}\text{s}^{-2} = 10^{7}\,\text{g cm}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}\)

So \(1\,\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2} = 10^{7}\,\text{g cm}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}\).

A light year is the distance light travels in one year. Using \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and, from Table 1.2, \(1\,\text{y} = 3.156 \times 10^{7}\,\text{s}\):

\(1\,\text{ly} = c \times 1\,\text{y} = (3 \times 10^{8})(3.156 \times 10^{7}) = 9.47 \times 10^{15}\,\text{m}\)

Taking the reciprocal,

\(1\,\text{m} = \dfrac{1}{9.47 \times 10^{15}}\,\text{ly} = 1.06 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{ly}\)

So \(1\,\text{m} \approx 1.06 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{ly}\), i.e. of the order of \(10^{-16}\,\text{ly}\).

Convert the metre and the second separately, remembering that the time unit is SQUARED:

\(1\,\text{m} = 10^{-3}\,\text{km}\) and \(1\,\text{s} = \dfrac{1}{3600}\,\text{h}\), so \(\text{s}^{-2} = (3600)^{2}\,\text{h}^{-2}\).

\(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times (3600)^{2}\,\text{km h}^{-2} = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.296 \times 10^{7}\)

\(= 3.888 \times 10^{4}\,\text{km h}^{-2}\)

So \(3.0\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 3.9 \times 10^{4}\,\text{km h}^{-2}\) (2 significant figures).

The magnitude of a physical quantity is inversely proportional to the size of the unit used to measure it, so if the unit grows by a factor the numerical value shrinks by the same factor.

In SI, \(1\,\text{cal} = 4.2\,\text{J} = 4.2\,\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}\).

In the new system the units are \(\alpha\,\text{kg}\), \(\beta\,\text{m}\) and \(\gamma\,\text{s}\), so

\(1\,\text{kg} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha}\) new mass units, \(1\,\text{m} = \dfrac{1}{\beta}\) new length units, \(1\,\text{s} = \dfrac{1}{\gamma}\) new time units.

Substituting,

\(1\,\text{cal} = 4.2 \left(\dfrac{1}{\alpha}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\beta}\right)^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\right)^{-2} = 4.2\,\alpha^{-1}\beta^{-2}\gamma^{2}\)

The \(\gamma\) carries a POSITIVE exponent because the time unit appears to the power \(-2\) in the energy unit, and inverting it flips the sign.

Hence a calorie has magnitude \(4.2\,\alpha^{-1}\beta^{-2}\gamma^{2}\) in the new units, as required.

A quantity that carries dimensions has no absolute size: its numerical value depends entirely on the unit chosen, so 'large' or 'small' only means anything relative to a stated standard. An atomic radius of about \(10^{-10}\,\text{m}\) is a tiny number in metres but a huge one in fermi \((10^{-15}\,\text{m})\).

The statement is therefore INCOMPLETE and needs reframing, for example:

"An atom is very small compared with the tip of a pin" (or, more sharply, compared with the wavelength of visible light, \(\sim 5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\), which is some thousands of atomic diameters).

Speed is a dimensional quantity, so calling it 'great' is meaningless until a standard of comparison is named.

The statement is therefore INCOMPLETE and needs reframing, for example:

"A jet plane moves with a speed greater than that of a superfast train."

(A jet cruises at roughly \(200\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), which is fast beside a train but very slow beside light, \(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) — which is precisely why the comparison has to be stated.)

Mass is a dimensional quantity, so 'very large' needs a reference mass.

The statement is therefore INCOMPLETE and needs reframing, for example:

"The mass of Jupiter is very large compared with the mass of the Earth" (about 318 times as large).

Against the Sun, by contrast, Jupiter's mass is about \(1/1000\) — small. The same number is 'large' or 'small' according to the standard chosen.

A NUMBER of molecules is a pure count — it is dimensionless, and a dimensionless quantity may legitimately be called large, because it is implicitly compared with unity.

So this statement is already meaningful as it stands and needs NO reframing: the air in a room contains of the order of \(10^{27}\) molecules, a number enormous compared with 1.

This is exactly the exception the opening statement is careful to make — it restricts its claim to a DIMENSIONAL quantity. One may still sharpen the statement by naming a standard, e.g. "the air in this room contains far more molecules than there are in \(1\,\text{cm}^{3}\) of air at STP".

This statement already names its standard of comparison — the electron — so it is meaningful as it stands and needs NO reframing.

It is also correct: \(m_{p}/m_{e} \approx 1836\), a dimensionless ratio, and it is the fact that the comparison produces a pure number that makes 'much more massive' a meaningful claim.

This statement already names its standard of comparison — the speed of light — so it is meaningful as it stands and needs NO reframing.

It is also correct: \(v_{\text{sound}} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{2}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in air against \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), a ratio of about \(10^{-6}\) — again a pure number, which is what makes the comparison meaningful.

The new unit of length is defined so that the speed of light in vacuum is unity, i.e. light covers exactly ONE new unit of length in one second.

The time taken is

\(t = 8\,\text{min}\;20\,\text{s} = (8 \times 60) + 20 = 500\,\text{s}\)

Distance in the new units \(= \text{speed} \times \text{time} = 1 \times 500 = 500\).

The Sun-Earth distance is \(500\) new units of length.

(Note the numerical value of \(c\) never enters: choosing \(c = 1\) makes the distance numerically equal to the light travel time in seconds.)

It ships here as a free-response question with the printed choices carried in the stem rather than as a multiple-choice question — inventing a fourth option would fabricate content the book does not contain. The printed key answers "(c)"; the answer below names that option by its text.] The most precise device is the one with the SMALLEST least count, so compute the least count of each.

Vernier callipers, 20 divisions on the sliding scale (main scale division \(1\,\text{mm}\)):

\(\text{LC} = \dfrac{1\,\text{mm}}{20} = 0.05\,\text{mm} = 5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}\)

Screw gauge, pitch \(1\,\text{mm}\) and 100 circular-scale divisions:

\(\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{no. of divisions}} = \dfrac{1\,\text{mm}}{100} = 0.01\,\text{mm} = 1 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}\)

Optical instrument measuring to within one wavelength of light:

\(\text{LC} \approx \lambda \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

The optical instrument's least count is smaller by a factor of about 20 than the screw gauge's, so the optical instrument that can measure length to within a wavelength of light is the most precise device.

Magnification is the ratio of the observed (image) width to the real (object) width:

\(m = \dfrac{\text{observed width}}{\text{actual thickness}}\)

So

\(\text{actual thickness} = \dfrac{\text{observed width}}{m} = \dfrac{3.5\,\text{mm}}{100} = 0.035\,\text{mm}\)

The estimated thickness of the hair is \(0.035\,\text{mm} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}\).

(Averaging the 20 observations reduces the random error in the measured width; it does not change the magnification.)

A metre scale cannot resolve a single thread diameter (well below its \(1\,\text{mm}\) least count), so measure MANY diameters at once and divide.

Method: wind the thread tightly and closely around a cylindrical rod or pencil so that successive turns touch one another with no gaps and no overlaps. Count the number of turns \(n\), and with the metre scale measure the total length \(L\) of the wound portion.

Then each turn accounts for one thread diameter, so

\(d = \dfrac{L}{n}\)

The diameter of the thread is \(L/n\). Because the unavoidable \(\pm 1\,\text{mm}\) reading error in \(L\) is divided by \(n\), the error in \(d\) is \(n\) times smaller — so use as many turns as possible, and repeat the winding a few times and average.

The least count is

\(\text{LC} = \dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{no. of circular-scale divisions}} = \dfrac{1.0\,\text{mm}}{200} = 0.005\,\text{mm} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}\)

So increasing the number of divisions does reduce the least count in proportion, and in that arithmetic sense the instrument becomes finer.

But NO, the accuracy cannot be increased arbitrarily. Least count sets only the smallest division that can be READ; it is not the same as accuracy. As the divisions are crowded closer they can no longer be resolved by eye, and the reading becomes limited instead by errors that do not shrink at all: backlash and play in the screw, non-uniformity of the threads, the varying pressure applied by the operator, thermal expansion, and the observer's own judgement.

Beyond a point these dominate, so the measurement becomes more precise-looking without becoming more accurate.

Each individual reading carries a random error — of sign and size varying unpredictably from trial to trial — arising from the observer, the grip on the callipers and small irregularities of the rod.

When readings are averaged, positive and negative random deviations tend to cancel, and the uncertainty in the mean falls as

\(\sigma_{\text{mean}} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}}\)

Going from \(N = 5\) to \(N = 100\) reduces the uncertainty in the mean by a factor

\(\sqrt{\dfrac{100}{5}} = \sqrt{20} \approx 4.5\)

So the set of 100 measurements yields a mean about 4.5 times more reliable, which is why it is preferred.

(Note this helps only against RANDOM error: a systematic error, such as a zero error in the callipers, is not reduced by averaging at all.)

Areas scale as the SQUARE of the linear magnification, so find the areal ratio first and take its square root.

Convert the slide area to SI: \(1.75\,\text{cm}^{2} = 1.75 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\).

Areal magnification:

\(m_{\text{area}} = \dfrac{1.55\,\text{m}^{2}}{1.75 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}} = 8.857 \times 10^{3}\)

Linear magnification:

\(m = \sqrt{m_{\text{area}}} = \sqrt{8.857 \times 10^{3}} = 94.1\)

The linear magnification of the projector-screen arrangement is about \(94.1\) (dimensionless).

(The '\(35\,\text{mm}\)' is the name of the slide format and plays no part in the calculation.)

In \(0.007\,\text{m}^{2}\) the number is less than 1, so the zeros to the right of the decimal point but to the LEFT of the first non-zero digit are not significant — they only fix the decimal place. Only the digit 7 is significant.

Number of significant figures = \(1\).

In \(2.64 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}\) the power of 10 is irrelevant to the count of significant figures; only the digits of the base number 2.64 count, and all three are non-zero.

Number of significant figures = \(3\).

In \(0.2370\,\text{g cm}^{-3}\) the leading zero before the decimal point is never significant, but the digits 2, 3, 7 are, and the TRAILING zero is significant because the number carries a decimal point.

Number of significant figures = \(4\).

In \(6.320\,\text{J}\) the digits 6, 3, 2 are non-zero and therefore significant, and the trailing zero is significant because the number has a decimal point.

Number of significant figures = \(4\).

In \(6.032\,\text{N m}^{-2}\) the zero lies BETWEEN two non-zero digits, and such a zero is always significant, wherever the decimal point falls.

Number of significant figures = \(4\).

In \(0.0006032\,\text{m}^{2}\) the number is less than 1, so the leading zeros (before the 6) are not significant. The significant digits are 6, 0, 3, 2 — the zero between 6 and 3 counts because it lies between two non-zero digits.

Number of significant figures = \(4\).

Work in metres: \(l = 4.234\,\text{m}\), \(b = 1.005\,\text{m}\), \(t = 2.01\,\text{cm} = 0.0201\,\text{m}\).

The sheet is a rectangular slab, so its (total) surface area is

\(S = 2(lb + bt + tl)\)

\(lb = 4.25517\,\text{m}^{2}\), \(bt = 0.0202005\,\text{m}^{2}\), \(tl = 0.0851034\,\text{m}^{2}\)

\(S = 2(4.25517 + 0.0202005 + 0.0851034) = 8.7209\,\text{m}^{2}\)

Volume:

\(V = l\,b\,t = 4.234 \times 1.005 \times 0.0201 = 0.0855289\,\text{m}^{3}\)

By the multiplication rule the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor, and \(t = 2.01\,\text{cm}\) has only 3.

Area \(= 8.72\,\text{m}^{2}\); Volume \(= 0.0855\,\text{m}^{3}\).

solution:
Both masses are stated to the same precision, so subtract directly:

\(\Delta m = 20.17\,\text{g} - 20.15\,\text{g} = 0.02\,\text{g}\)

For subtraction the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest; both have 2, so the answer is quoted to 2 decimal places.

The difference in the masses of the two pieces is \(0.02\,\text{g}\).

(Note that although each mass was known to 4 significant figures, their difference has only 1 — subtracting two nearly equal numbers destroys significant figures, which is exactly why the rule for addition and subtraction is stated in decimal places rather than significant figures.)

Use the principle of homogeneity of dimensions. A quantity that is subtracted from the pure number 1 must itself be dimensionless, so the bracket \(\left(1 - v^{2}\right)\) as written is dimensionally inconsistent: \(v^{2}\) has dimensions \([\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]\), which cannot be subtracted from a dimensionless 1.

To make \(v^{2}\) dimensionless it must be divided by another quantity with the dimensions of speed squared, and the only such quantity available is the speed of light \(c\). Since

\(\left[\dfrac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}\right] = \dfrac{[\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]}{[\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]} = [\text{M}^{0}\text{L}^{0}\text{T}^{0}]\)

the missing \(c\) belongs under \(v^{2}\), as \(c^{2}\).

The correct relation is

\(m = \dfrac{m_{0}}{\left(1 - v^{2}/c^{2}\right)^{1/2}} = m_{0}\left(1 - \dfrac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)^{-1/2}\)

Take the quoted size of the hydrogen atom as its radius, \(r = 0.5\,\text{Å} = 0.5 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m} = 5 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\), and treat the atom as a sphere.

Volume of one atom:

\(V_{1} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (5 \times 10^{-11})^{3} = 5.24 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

One mole contains \(N_{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms, so the total atomic volume is

\(V = N_{A} V_{1} = (6.022 \times 10^{23})(5.24 \times 10^{-31}) = 3.15 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

The atomic volume of a mole of hydrogen atoms is about \(3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^{3}\).

Take the quoted size of the hydrogen molecule as its radius, \(r = 1\,\text{Å} = 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\), and treat the molecule as a sphere.

Volume of one molecule:

\(V_{1} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (10^{-10})^{3} = 4.19 \times 10^{-30}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

Atomic (molecular) volume of one mole:

\(V_{a} = N_{A}V_{1} = (6.022 \times 10^{23})(4.19 \times 10^{-30}) = 2.52 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

Molar volume \(V_{m} = 22.4\,\text{L} = 22.4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{3}\).

Ratio:

\(\dfrac{V_{m}}{V_{a}} = \dfrac{22.4 \times 10^{-3}}{2.52 \times 10^{-6}} = 8.9 \times 10^{3} \approx 10^{4}\)

The ratio is about \(10^{4}\).

It is so large because in a gas the molecules are separated by distances far greater than their own size: the intermolecular separation at STP is roughly ten times the molecular diameter, and since volume goes as the cube of a length this gives about \(10^{3}\)-\(10^{4}\) times more room than the molecules themselves occupy. The molecules fill only a tiny fraction of the container, which is why an ideal gas is so compressible.

What the eye registers is not linear displacement but the ANGLE an object subtends at the eye, and the rate at which that angle changes.

For an object at perpendicular distance \(r\) from the track, while the train moves with speed \(v\) the line of sight turns at the angular rate

\(\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}\)

so \(\omega\) is inversely proportional to the distance of the object.

For nearby trees and houses \(r\) is small (a few metres to a few hundred metres), so \(\omega\) is large: their line of sight swings quickly backwards, and they appear to rush past in the direction opposite to the train's motion.

For distant objects — hill tops, the Moon, the stars — \(r\) is enormous (the Moon is \(\sim 3.8 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m}\) away), so \(\omega\) is almost zero over the whole journey. Their direction relative to the observer barely changes, and they appear stationary. Because the observer knows he himself is moving while these objects hold a fixed direction, they seem to travel along with him.

This is simply parallax: the apparent shift of an object against its background falls off as \(1/r\).

Expectation first: although the Sun is a plasma, and a gas at ordinary pressure has a density of order \(1\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), the Sun's enormous self-gravity compresses its material, so one should expect its MEAN density to lie in the range of solids and liquids \((\sim 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3})\) rather than that of gases.

Check this with the data. Treating the Sun as a sphere of radius \(R = 7.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m}\):

\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (7.0 \times 10^{8})^{3} = 1.44 \times 10^{27}\,\text{m}^{3}\)

With \(M = 2.0 \times 10^{30}\,\text{kg}\),

\(\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{30}}{1.44 \times 10^{27}} = 1.4 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)

The mean mass density of the Sun is \(1.4 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), which is of the same order as water \((10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3})\) and about a thousand times that of a gas at ordinary conditions.

So the guess is correct: the Sun's density lies in the range of solids and liquids, not gases. The high density despite the ionized, gaseous state arises from the inward gravitational attraction of the outer layers on the inner ones.
